newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--Distillate stocks seen edging up in APIs.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--Distillate stocks seen edging up in APIs.

text.p: Forecasts for a cold spell in many U.S. regions had the market fearing Monday that distillate demand may start outstripping output, but a small build in distillate stocks is expected in this week's oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API).

"Expect distillate production to remain near record levels while demand should have slipped during the week," said Thomas Blakeslee, analyst with Cargill Investor Services. An average of trader estimates by Reuters shows distillate stocks building by 500,000 barrels for the week ended December 13.

Estimates of distillate stocks, which are comprised of heating oil and diesel, ranged from a draw of 1.5 million barrels to a build of two million barrels, but dealers said last week's mild weather and distributor liquidation of their lower priced heating oil stocks dampened distillate buying from refiners. The data will be released Tuesday evening.

Distillate ouput was supposed to remain around a high 3.66 million barrels a day (bpd) seen the week of December 6. The general refinery run rate is expected to stay near the breakneck pace of 94.2 percent, cutting into crude stocks which should rise overall due to a strong pace in imports.
"The arb is a bit more attractive (from the North Sea), and I expect imports to be near 7.8 million barrels," said Sweeney Oil trader Jim Ritterbusch.
Estimates for crude stocks ranged from down a half million barrels to up 1.5 million barrels, with the average yielding a build of one million barrels.

Imports from Europe are also expected to have boosted gasoline stocks again, after imports rose by almost 200,000 barrels a week ago. Dealers noted historically high gasoline output of 8.12 million bpd in last week's data should decline by several hundred thousand.
"You just can't keep that up," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown, of the gasoline production rate.
There could be a surprise to the upside in the distillate stock build, said dealers, expecting little stock movement to have occurred from primary to secondary levels.

"Distributors were more concerned with liquidation than buying after the price declines," said Sweeney Oil's Ritterbusch, explaining a decline several weeks ago in heating oil prices left retailers brimming with lower priced stocks ahead of winter.

"There had already been a lot of primary to secondary stock movement earlier in the season," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt, adding the heating oil retailer had not been ready to restock last week.
